episode.lensDescription: Practical implementation strategies and actionable insights
episode.broadcastScript:
This is The Innovation Pulse for Wednesday, March 18, 2026. And here's who is innovating in higher education today.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In Insights and Trends today, more colleges and universities are adding artificial intelligence majors to their curriculum. According to USA Today, Northwestern University announced the creation of a new A.I. major on March 9, with enrollment available beginning in the fall 2026 semester. Northwestern joins a growing list of institutions offering dedicated A.I. degrees, with Carnegie Mellon University having launched the first undergraduate A.I. degree back in 2018. The major aims to prepare students to lead in a rapidly evolving field, teaching machine learning, natural language processing, A.I. systems and infrastructure, and the mathematical foundations of modern A.I. Students will also learn about the human and societal dimensions of the technology, including privacy, sustainability, and intellectual property. Schools including the University of Arizona, Purdue University, M.I.T., and U.C. San Diego also offer A.I. programs. At Purdue, students can choose between a Bachelor of Arts that examines A.I. ethics and societal impacts, or a Bachelor of Science focused on building A.I. machines.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Turning to Case Study, faculty at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill are embracing A.I. in their teaching and research. According to UNC, faculty across multiple schools are working to ensure students are literate in artificial intelligence while also integrating A.I. into their own scholarly work. The initiative spans the university's colleges and professional schools, with faculty developing approaches to incorporate A.I. tools responsibly into coursework.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In Investing in Innovation, the City University of New York system is expanding its use of A.I. in teaching and student support with a three million dollar investment. According to GovTech, the funding supports one hundred thirteen A.I. initiatives across CUNY campuses through a one-year innovation fund, part of Governor Kathy Hochul's effort to position New York as a leader in A.I. The projects focus on four areas: student and academic support, courses, ethical and social implications, and literacy. At Borough of Manhattan Community College, A.I. will be integrated into an introductory computing course taken by thousands of students each year. Hostos Community College will include A.I. instruction in its first-year seminar for incoming students. Brooklyn College is using automated systems to analyze usage data and optimize inventory at food pantries to address student food insecurity. Another initiative at CUNY Graduate School of Public Health will create an A.I. powered navigator to help students find mental health resources and legal support.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In Ethical A.I. today, professors across Georgia are returning to traditional blue book exams as a response to A.I. powered cheating. According to the Atlanta Journal Constitution, university professors are embracing these handwritten exam booklets not for nostalgia, but as a practical countermeasure against students using A.I. tools to complete assignments. The shift reflects ongoing challenges faculty face in maintaining academic integrity as A.I. writing tools become more sophisticated and harder to detect.

<break time="1.0s"/>

That's today's Innovation Pulse. Full coverage and source links at innovating higher ed dot com.

quickHits.headline: Georgia Professors Return to Blue Book Exams to Combat A.I. Cheating
quickHits.summary: University professors across Georgia are returning to traditional blue book exams as a response to A.I.-powered cheating. According to the Atlanta Journal-Constitution, professors are embracing these handwritten exam booklets not for nostalgia, but as a practical countermeasure against students using A.I. tools to complete assignments. The shift reflects ongoing challenges faculty face in maintaining academic integrity as A.I. writing tools become more sophisticated and harder to detect. The blue book, a staple of higher education for decades, offers a low-tech solution that ensures student work is completed in person without digital assistance.

quickHits.headline: Austin Community College Receives $875,000 Grant for A.I. Initiative
quickHits.summary: Austin Community College District has announced a partnership with the Trellis Foundation that includes an $875,000 grant for its Digital Twin Initiative. According to Spectrum News, the initiative will use A.I. to proactively support students by connecting them to services like advising, tutoring, and mental health resources in real time. ACC Chancellor Russell Lowery-Hart explained the approach: "Take all of the data points that we have on our students and make them immediately actionable so that instead of waiting for the student to identify a need and then try to find that need fulfilled, we could know when they have the need in real time." Small business owners will also be able to access training on using A.I. to expand their businesses. Additionally, ACC will offer an electrical technician certification to meet demands of the growing data center industry in Texas.

quickHits.headline: MIT-IBM Watson AI Lab Accelerates Early-Career Faculty Research
quickHits.summary: Five MIT faculty members describe how early engagement with the MIT-IBM Watson AI Lab has shaped their research careers. According to MIT News, the academia-industry collaboration has provided computing resources, intellectual support, and partnerships that helped faculty establish their research groups. Jacob Andreas, associate professor in EECS, credits the lab with launching his work on natural language processing during a pivotal moment when the field was undergoing significant shifts. Yoon Kim, also in EECS, describes the relationship as "completely transformative" for his research on large language model capabilities. The collaboration has allowed faculty including Justin Solomon, Chuchu Fan, and Faez Ahmed to pursue multi-year projects spanning robotics, geometric machine learning, and engineering design.

quickHits.headline: Research Shows Which Jobs Face A.I. Disruption—and Who Can Adapt
quickHits.summary: New research from GovAI and the Brookings Institution estimates which workers may be most and least able to adapt if A.I. transforms their jobs. According to the Washington Post, researchers found that many people most at risk if A.I. transforms work are also best placed to find new jobs. However, approximately 6.1 million largely clerical and administrative workers scored high for both A.I. exposure and low adaptability. Women make up about 86 percent of these most vulnerable workers. The researchers measured adaptability based on education, varied work experience, wealth, age under 55, and living in cities with plentiful jobs.
